The other half was pure dread: what if nobody picks me, what if I freeze, what will Papa say? The dread was vague and huge. So I did something my senior Meenal suggested. I wrote the dread down as a list. "Freeze in interviews" became "do three mock interviews". "No company picks me" became "apply to twelve, not four". "Papa" became "talk to Papa this Sunday". I went to my faculty mentor with the list, and she helped me pick which companies suited me. Each small step made the dread smaller. I still felt nervous on the day. But it was nervous with a plan.

He called a senior who had studied there, and they talked for an hour. After that he ticked something off the chart almost every day. The night before he left, he said, "I'm still scared. Week two. She went to her tutor, Gautam sir, and admitted she was stuck. He didn't lecture. He asked her to split each subject into topics and write them on index cards, then pick three cards a day. "Just three. Not the whole mountain." She tried it. The first day she finished two. The second, three.
Week four. The night before the first exam, she still felt butterflies. But the index card box was almost empty, and she'd made notes for each topic. She texted Gautam sir: "Still nervous. But it feels like the good kind now." He replied, "Good. Nervous means you care. Sleep."

They sat quietly. Then Clara said, "Let's split the lecture notes. You take the first half, I'll do the second. And maybe ask the café to move one shift?" Vera nodded slowly. You asked how the new semester is going, and I didn't want to just say "fine" again.
Honestly, I'm bored in some classes and exhausted in all of them. In the economics lecture I doodle the whole time. In the evening I scroll for an hour and then feel guilty. I thought I'd become lazy.
Then last week the college nurse asked how much I sleep. Five hours, most nights. She said that alone could make every lecture feel dull.
So I'm trying a few things. Phone out of the room at night. Bed by eleven. A short walk after lunch. In the dull lecture, I've started writing one question for the teacher every fifteen minutes, just to stay with it.
It's only been four days, but I yawn less. Will tell you more on Sunday's call.
Love,
Shalini

Hrithik gave his first competition speech today. Before he went on, I saw his hands shaking so much the cue cards rattled, and he kept wiping his palms on his trousers. He told me, "I'm going to mess this up. My body's telling me I'm not ready." I said, "Your body's telling you this matters. That's energy. Let's use it." By the second minute his hands had steadied. His teammate Vishal told me afterwards that Hrithik has been having these shakes before every small class presentation, not just big events, and sometimes can't sleep the night before. I've suggested he talk to the college counsellor as well, and he's agreed to go on Friday.

subtype: Direct versus indirect communication across cultures [Mismatch]
passage: It was the last day of the project handover, and the office in Bengaluru was chaos: two clients calling, a server down. Tejas's new manager, Ankita, who had just moved from the Berlin office, walked up to his desk. "Your report has three errors. Fix them by four." Then she walked off. Tejas sat stunned. At his previous team, a manager would have said, "Maybe we could look at a few small things?" This felt like a slap. He wanted to complain. With forty minutes left, he didn't have time to brood. He fixed the errors. Then he walked to her desk. "Ankita, can I ask something? When you said the report had errors, were you upset with me?" She looked surprised. "No! I was just saying what needed doing. In Berlin that's normal. Should I say it differently?" Tejas smiled. "Maybe add a 'please'. I'll get used to the directness." "Deal," she said.

qa.q: By what time did Ankita want the errors fixed?
qa.a: By four.

qa.q: What was Tejas feeling when Ankita walked off?
qa.a: He felt stunned and hurt, as if slapped, because he was used to softer, indirect feedback.

qa.q: What did Tejas do that helped under time pressure?
qa.a: He fixed the errors first, then kindly asked Ankita whether she was upset, instead of brooding or complaining.

qa.q: How did Ankita see her own direct words?
qa.a: She saw them as just saying what needed doing, normal where she came from, and she was willing to adjust.

grounding: Shows a young adult meeting a direct communicator after working with indirect ones and asking a kind clarifying question.

subtype: Direct versus indirect communication across cultures [Mismatch]
passage: Yusuf and his flatmate Nazia had shared a flat in Mumbai for a month when Yusuf noticed something. Whenever he asked if she minded his cousin staying over, she'd say, "Up to you," and go quiet. When he asked about the music at night, she'd say, "It's fine, it's fine." But she seemed tired and cool afterwards. Yusuf's own family said everything plainly, sometimes loudly. He was confused. Was she angry? Did "fine" mean fine? One Sunday over breakfast, he asked. "Nazia, I think I might be missing your hints. When you say 'up to you', do you actually mind?" Nazia put her cup down and laughed, a little embarrassed. "Honestly? Yes. I grew up where saying no directly is rude." "And I grew up where hints go straight over my head," Yusuf said. They agreed: she'd try saying it plainly, and he'd ask when unsure.

qa.q: How long had Yusuf and Nazia shared the flat?
qa.a: For a month.

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling when she said "Up to you" and went quiet?
qa.a: She was uncomfortable and minded, but felt that saying no directly would be rude.

qa.q: What did Yusuf do that helped?
qa.a: He asked kindly and directly whether her "up to you" meant she minded, instead of guessing.

qa.q: How did Yusuf's own family background shape how he read Nazia?
qa.a: His family said everything plainly, so her hints went over his head and left him confused.

grounding: Shows two young adults with direct and indirect styles finding that neither is better and asking clarifying questions kindly.

subtype: Sustained displays and emotional load [Regulating]
passage: Harsha, you think nobody notices when you're worn out. Let your Rafiq chacha tell you about my own bad year. I was twenty-one, working at a garage in Bhopal by day and studying for a diploma by night, while my father was in and out of hospital. For three months I snapped at everyone. My face went grey. I answered my mother in single words. I thought I was hiding it. My friend Sameer finally sat me down at the chai stall. "You've been like this since March. Not one day, but months." I laughed it off. He didn't. "Go see the doctor at the clinic. Just to talk." I didn't want to. But I went. The doctor listened and told me to sleep more, drop one shift, and talk to a counsellor at the hospital where my father was. I did. It took weeks, but the grey went out of my face. Rest isn't weakness, beta.

qa.q: Where did young Rafiq work by day?
qa.a: At a garage in Bhopal.

qa.q: How was young Rafiq feeling during those three months?
qa.a: He was worn out and stressed, snapping at everyone and answering in single words, though he thought he was hiding it.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped Rafiq?
qa.a: Sameer refused to let him laugh it off and urged him to see the doctor, who advised rest, fewer shifts and counselling.

qa.q: How did Sameer see Rafiq's months of irritability?
qa.a: He saw it as a long-lasting sign of strain, not a bad day, that needed rest and help.

grounding: Shows a young adult whose weeks of stress show as a grey face, short answers and irritability, and how rest and help relieve it.

subtype: Sustained displays and emotional load [Regulating]
passage: Varun had been working double shifts at the call centre for five weeks, covering for a colleague on leave, while finishing his final-year project. His flatmate Sarita noticed the signs: dark circles, one-word replies, snapping when she asked about dinner. Tonight he came home at midnight, slammed his bag down and said, "Don't talk to me." Sarita didn't argue. The next morning, with only ten minutes before he left, she made him tea and said, "Varun, you've been like this for weeks. Not a bad day. Weeks." He stared at the tea. "I can't stop. The project's due in two weeks." "Then can you drop one shift? Or ask your project guide for help?" He was quiet. "I'm so tired, Sarita." "I know. There's a counsellor at your college, too." That evening he told his team lead he'd do single shifts only, and booked a slot with the counsellor for Thursday.

qa.q: How long had Varun been working double shifts?
qa.a: For five weeks.

qa.q: What was Varun feeling when he admitted "I'm so tired"?
qa.a: He was exhausted and overwhelmed after weeks of double shifts and project work.

qa.q: What steps helped Varun lighten the load?
qa.a: Dropping to single shifts and booking a counsellor, after Sarita named the pattern of weeks.

qa.q: How did Sarita read Varun's snapping?
qa.a: She saw it as a sign of weeks of strain, not personal rudeness, so she didn't argue and spoke to him calmly.

grounding: Shows a young adult carrying stress for weeks, visible in tiredness and irritability, and responding with rest and support.

subtype: Sustained displays and emotional load [Regulating]
passage: In the Kolkata design office, Arnab noticed that his colleague Naveen had stopped joining the lunch table weeks ago. His face was drawn every day now, not just on deadline days. He answered questions with "Hmm" or "Later", and twice he snapped at the intern over small things. Arnab wasn't sure what was going on. It could be family, work, health. On Friday, he asked Naveen to step out for chai. "I'm not trying to pry. You've seemed really tired for a while. Weeks. Is it work?" Naveen rubbed his eyes. "It's my mother's illness. I've been driving to Howrah every night." "That's a lot." Arnab paused. "Can you tell the manager? And our company has a counselling line." Naveen nodded slowly. "I didn't think anyone noticed." On Monday he told the manager, who gave him flexible hours for a month.

qa.q: Where had Naveen been driving every night?
qa.a: To Howrah.

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling during those weeks?
qa.a: He was exhausted and strained from his mother's illness, which showed in his drawn face and snapping.

qa.q: What did Arnab do that helped?
qa.a: He named the long-lasting signs gently, asked privately, and suggested telling the manager and using the counselling line.

qa.q: How did the manager respond when Naveen explained?
qa.a: The manager gave him flexible hours for a month.

grounding: Shows a young adult noticing a colleague's weeks-long tiredness and irritability and encouraging rest and support.

subtype: Expressionless while excited or anxious [Mismatch]
passage:
"Himani," Thomas said, kneeling on the beach, holding out a small box. "Will you marry me?"
Himani looked at the ring. Her face didn't move. Not a smile, not a tear.
Thomas's hands started to shake. "You can say no. It's okay. I..."
"Thomas."
"I rushed it, didn't I? Your parents, and"
"Thomas. Stop." Her voice was very quiet. "Yes."
He stared. "You look like you're at a funeral."
"I know. When I feel something this big, my face goes blank. It's like my body's holding on."
"So you're happy?"
"I'm so happy I can't breathe properly." Her hand was shaking as she held it out. "Put it on before I faint."
He laughed, still shaky, and slid it on. Then her face finally cracked into a smile, and she started crying.
"Next time, blink or something," he said. "I almost died."

qa.q: Where did Thomas propose?
qa.a: On the beach.

qa.q: What was Himani feeling behind her blank face?
qa.a: She was so happy and overwhelmed she couldn't breathe properly, and her face went blank as her body held on.

qa.q: What did Thomas nearly get wrong, and what helped?
qa.a: He read her blank face as a no; listening when she asked him to stop and explain helped.

qa.q: What was it like for Thomas while Himani's face stayed blank?
qa.a: He panicked, hands shaking, sure he had rushed it and she would say no.

grounding: Shows a young adult keeping a blank face during a proposal while feeling great excitement, and a partner learning not to assume indifference.

subtype: Expressionless while excited or anxious [Mismatch]
passage: On results day in my final year, the whole class crowded round the notice board. I'm Tarun. When I found my name at the top of the list, I just stood there. My face did nothing. Inside, my heart was going like a drum, and I wanted to shout. But I've always frozen when feelings get too big. My friend Sachin, who'd barely passed, looked at me and said, "Aren't you happy? You topped!" His voice was a bit sharp. I think he thought I didn't care, or that I was showing off by being cool about it. I didn't know what to say. That night I messaged him: "Sorry about today. I was so happy I couldn't move my face. And I'm really glad you passed." He replied, "Oh. I thought you were being snooty." We laughed about it later. Now I tell people: blank face, busy heart.

qa.q: Where did Tarun find his name?
qa.a: At the top of the list.

qa.q: What was Tarun feeling on results day?
qa.a: Tarun was thrilled, heart going like a drum and wanting to shout, even though the face stayed blank.

qa.q: What did Tarun do to repair the misunderstanding with Sachin?
qa.a: Tarun messaged to explain the blank face came from being overwhelmed with happiness, and congratulated Sachin on passing.

qa.q: How did Sachin read Tarun's blank face?
qa.a: He thought Tarun didn't care or was being snooty, especially since Sachin had barely passed.

grounding: Shows a young adult with an expressionless face on results day while excited inside, and a friend misreading it as indifference.

subtype: Expressionless while excited or anxious [Mismatch]
passage:
Class teacher's note, final-year results day, Friday.
When the results were displayed, most students screamed or cried or hugged. Rajni stood completely still in front of the board, face blank, for almost a minute. Her friend Ira came to me worried. "Ma'am, is Rajni okay? She doesn't look happy. She's got a distinction." I went over quietly. Rajni's hands were trembling, and her breathing was fast, though her face showed nothing. I asked softly, "How are you feeling?" She whispered, "I don't know yet. I'm scared it's a mistake." We checked her marks together on the official sheet. Only then did she smile, very slowly. I told Ira later that a blank face often means someone is holding a lot inside, not that they don't care. I've made a note to check on Rajni again next week; she tends to hold her feelings very tightly.
— Mrs Fernandes

qa.q: What result did Rajni get?
qa.a: A distinction.

qa.q: What was Rajni feeling behind her blank face?
qa.a: She was anxious and overwhelmed, scared the result was a mistake, with trembling hands and fast breathing.

qa.q: What did Mrs Fernandes do that helped Rajni?
qa.a: She went over quietly, asked how Rajni felt, and checked the official marks with her before Rajni could believe it.

qa.q: How did Ira read Rajni's blank face?
qa.a: Ira worried Rajni wasn't happy or wasn't okay, since she showed no expression despite a distinction.

grounding: Shows a young adult keeping a blank face on results day while anxious and excited inside, and a teacher explaining it isn't indifference.

subtype: Speaking politely while angry in formal settings [Regulating]
passage: At the college fee office in Pune, Sarika had been waiting in line for an hour when the clerk, Uday, told her that her scholarship hadn't been applied and she'd have to pay the full fee by Friday. It was the third time she'd come about the same error. Her face burned; her fists clenched under the counter. She wanted to shout. She took a breath. "Uday-ji, I understand this isn't your fault. But I've brought the scholarship letter three times now. Could you please check with the accounts head today and give me a written note that the fee is on hold?" Her voice was steady, though her heart pounded. Uday looked at the letter, sighed and made a call. Ten minutes later, he handed her a signed note. Outside, Sarika called her brother and ranted for five whole minutes. Then she laughed and went to class.

qa.q: How many times had Sarika come about the same error?
qa.a: The third time.

qa.q: What was Sarika feeling at the counter?
qa.a: She was angry and frustrated, face burning and fists clenched, though she kept her voice calm.

qa.q: What made Sarika's request effective?
qa.a: It was polite but firm, acknowledged it wasn't Uday's fault, and asked for a specific action and a written note.

qa.q: How did Uday respond to Sarika's calm, firm request?
qa.a: He sighed, checked the letter, called the accounts head and gave her a signed note.

grounding: Shows a young adult staying courteous but firm while angry in a service dispute, and venting afterwards in a healthy way.

subtype: Speaking politely while angry in formal settings [Regulating]
passage:
Dear Zainab,
You asked how the flight home went. Badly, and then better.
They cancelled my flight and put me on one twelve hours later. At the counter, the agent kept saying "policy, sir" and wouldn't look at me. I was furious. My hands shook. I wanted to shout that I had an exam the next morning.
Instead I said, very quietly, "I understand you didn't cancel it. I need to be in Delhi by morning for an exam. Could you check the 6 p.m. flight, or give me a meal voucher and a hotel in writing?" He paused, then found me a seat at 6.
I was polite the whole time. But afterwards I walked round the terminal twice, fast, and called Ammi and complained for ten minutes. That helped more than shouting would have.
Your bhai,
Imran

qa.q: How much later was the flight Imran was first put on?
qa.a: Twelve hours later.

qa.q: What was Imran feeling at the airline counter?
qa.a: He was furious, his hands shaking, and wanted to shout about his exam.

qa.q: What made Imran's approach work?
qa.a: He stayed quiet and polite, acknowledged it wasn't the agent's fault, and made a specific, firm request with options.

qa.q: How did the agent respond to Imran's calm request?
qa.a: He paused, then found Imran a seat on the 6 p.m. flight.

grounding: Shows a young adult speaking politely while angry in a service dispute, using a firm request and a healthy outlet afterwards.

subtype: Speaking politely while angry in formal settings [Regulating]
passage: Zubin, you asked on your podcast about staying calm when you're boiling inside. I'm Neelam. Last Diwali, at the family dinner, my Mama started joking about my job at the animal shelter. "Neelam cleans dog cages with a degree. Waste of money!" Everyone laughed. My face went hot. I wanted to throw my plate. Instead I smiled, put my spoon down and said, very politely, "Mama, I love my work. I'd like you not to joke about it in front of everyone." There was a small silence. Mama cleared his throat and said, "Okay, okay." Then my mother changed the subject. I stayed polite for the rest of the evening. But after dinner I went for a long walk and called my friend Shreya and let it all out, every angry word. I think the calm, firm line worked because I didn't have to explode at the table. I exploded later, on a walk, where it hurt nobody.

qa.q: Where does Neelam work?
qa.a: At the animal shelter.

qa.q: What was Neelam feeling when Mama joked about the job?
qa.a: Neelam felt angry and humiliated, face hot, wanting to throw the plate.

qa.q: What made Neelam's response work?
qa.a: A calm, polite but firm request that stated what Neelam wanted, followed by a healthy outlet later with a friend.

qa.q: How did Mama react to Neelam's request?
qa.a: He paused, cleared his throat and said "Okay, okay", suggesting he felt a little embarrassed and backed down.

grounding: Shows a young adult staying courteous while angry at a family gathering, using a calm firm request and venting in a healthy way later.
